extracted.intended_audience: 17th-century natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and readers of the Philosophical Transactions (physicians, surgeons, opticians, astronomers)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and experimentally investigating natural-philosophical questions (medical remedies, optics/colours, instrument design, astronomical observations) using witnessed trials, controlled experiments, and geometrical/instrumental descriptions. Emphasizes experimental method, replication, and matching theoretical claims to empirical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical efficacy indicators for a haemostatic remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures and observations used to judge the success of the new astringent liquor applied to amputated limbs: that the blood was staunched without any other dressing; patient was free from pain; patient slept soon after and during the night; no return of bleeding; no eschar or disfiguring wound; patient found herself/himself better and better with no ill accident since.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: two human amputations (woman and seaman) where arteries dressed with linen pledgets dipped in the essence and bandaged — blood stopped quickly and patients slept; three calves with legs cut off stopped bleeding in four minutes. Emphasizes short stopping time, absence of secondary injury (eschar), subjective relief (pain and sleep), and continued good outcome. Also implies value of following patients 'ever since' to detect delayed ill effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration by witnessed trials and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental demonstrations should be conducted in the presence of qualified observers and be replicable: physicians and chirurgeons were sent to be present and to 'faithfully report', and trials were repeated on multiple subjects (humans and calves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The King ordered physicians present at the hospital and later caused the preparation to be made in his laboratory and dispatched to the fleet; trials were carried out on three calves in Whitehall. Guidance implies importance of independent witnesses, faithful reporting to authorities, and replication on multiple specimens (including animals) to convince sceptics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls for colour-mixing experiments (dark room and exclusion of extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing whether a subset of prism colours will compose white, perform the experiment in a darkened room, cast prism colours on a white surface, and prevent the extreme colours (red and purple) from striking the surface so only intermediate colours (yellow, green, blue) remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Parisian correspondent suggests Mr. Newton's proposed experiment: 'receiving against a wall of a darkened room the colours of the prism, and to cast their reflected light on white paper. Here you must hinder the colours of the extremities, viz. the red and purple, from striking against the wall, and leave only the intermediate colours ...' Also warns that reflections weaken coloured light so experiments must control stray scattering light; anti-pattern: performing in insufficient darkness or allowing stray reflected light that dilutes colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise method for investigating the nature of colours (resolve, examine, recombine)
rubrics_metrics.description: To examine the nature of colours: first resolve light into colours as far as practicable, examine the properties of those separated colours individually, then try reconjoining two or more (or all) and finally separate them again to observe what changes recombination produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent states this is tedious but necessary: 'resolve light into colours, and then by examining the properties of those colours apart, and afterwards by trying the effects of re-conjoining two or more, or all of those, and lastly, by separating them again, to examine what changes that re-conjunction had wrought in them.' This is presented as a methodological rubric for rigorous experimental investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for equivalence of different 'whites'
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a white made from two colours is equivalent to the sun's white (or ordinary white objects), it is not enough that it 'to the naked eye shall appear like other whites'; it must 'agree with them in all other properties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues that a white produced by combining two colours must match the sun's white under further tests — e.g., when viewed through a prism it must decompose into the same continuous series of colours. The guidance: demonstrate equivalence across multiple experimental probes (prism decomposition, reflexibility, refrangibility), not merely superficial appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical requirements any account of colours must meet
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and propositions that a satisfactory theory must address: definitions of homogeneal (uniform) vs heterogeneal light; that simple (homogeneal) colours are exhibited by homogeneal light; propositions such as 'The sun's light consists of rays differing by indefinite degrees of refrangibility' and 'There are as many simple or homogeneal colours as degrees of refrangibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lays out explicit definitions and propositions as standards a theory should match: explain refrangibility, why whiteness of sunlight requires an indefinite variety of primitive colours, and why refraction separates pre-existing ray qualities rather than creating them. A theory that fails to account for these empirical propositions would be inadequate according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical demonstration that rays do not act on one another and refraction doesn't change ray qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically show (by experiment) that light rays do not act on one another in passing through the same medium and that rays suffer no change of their qualities (colour, refrangibility, reflexibility) from refraction or from the adjacent quiet medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton refers to experiments (Transactions p.23–27) as evidence; uses these propositions to argue that refraction separates rays rather than modifies them. Guidance: include direct experimental demonstrations that separate competing hypotheses (interaction vs non-interaction, alteration vs separation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for instrument construction and geometric alignment (prosopographic parallelogram)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumental and geometric requirements for the prosopographic parallelogram used to delineate attitudes and gestures: alignment so that the ray through hole O and the globule is perpendicular to the delineatory plane; ruler AR fitted perpendicularly; the central style fixed; sights PR and SV mounted; rays from object through sights to eye are parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The device description enumerates observations (1–3) establishing geometric relations (perpendicularity, definition of delineatory/rational planes, parallelism of rays). Guidance: follow the specified construction and alignment (central pin HF, index ruler, sights with hole and thread with globule) to ensure accurate proportional delineation; these are prescriptive construction criteria rather than evaluation scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and verification when claiming white from two colours (ensure colours are uncompounded)
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that two colours produce white, ensure that the two colours used are truly uncompounded (simple/homogeneal) and verify by attempting to resolve them into further simple colours; otherwise the apparent white may be an aggregate of many primitive colours disguised as two mixtures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Parisian correspondent warns that many successful 'two-colour' whites resulted from using colours that were themselves compounds (e.g., orange made of red/orange/yellow and blue of multiple blues and greens). Guidance: test each purported simple colour via prism/resolution to confirm its simplicity before using it to claim primitive composition; anti-pattern is to conflate compounded intermediate colours with primitive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescope/optical design must account for refrangibility aberration and ray density
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of refracting telescope performance must consider the aberration caused by different refrangibility of rays, the distribution of ray errors (middle parts vs perimeter), and the relative density of light at the image point so as to explain why pictures may still appear distinct despite irregular refraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton and correspondents discuss computing errors for glass and speculum, noting that central rays are refracted more accurately while extreme rays are few and weakened by scattering; suggested test: cover lens except for a small hole at the edge to measure colour breadth. Guidance: optical claims should be tested by calculation of ray errors and targeted instrumental experiments; anti-pattern: ignoring distribution (density) effects and only considering maximal lateral deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting astronomical observations (motions, periods, distances, parallax)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting observational astronomy (e.g., Jupiter's satellites, Mars), provide measured motions, periods, distances of satellites/planets, deduced parallaxes and derived solar distance estimates, and note accuracy relative to later observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Flamsteed's account reports motions, periods, distances and a derived parallax for Mars of 25" and a solar parallax estimate of about 10", with a note that this is too small by about a fifth according to later, more exact observations. Guidance: include numeric measures, error commentary, and comparisons to subsequent corrections.
